processing: Stems, leaves and flowers of oregano are simply air-dried, with no oxidation or roasting.
harvest_season: Usually gathered around flowering in summer, as with most aromatic herbs of the mint family. The plant blooms after the lime trees finish in Russia.
appearance_dry: Crumbled grey-green leaf, often with small flower heads and bits of stem.
appearance_liquor: Clear yellow to light amber, as with most dried aromatic herbs.
appearance_wet: Soft, dark green leaf fragments and flower heads.
taste_profile: Savoury and sharply aromatic, the smell of the kitchen herb in a thinner, warmer form; turns bitter if steeped long.

brewing.notes: Western-style: about a tablespoon of whole dried leaf per cup, steeped 5 minutes, up to 10 for strength. Whole leaf gives a cleaner cup than ground oregano. Honey and lemon both suit it.

vintage_note: Sold as a dried herb, not by year; the same dried oregano often serves both kitchen and teapot. As with other dried aromatic herbs, the current season's picking smells strongest. Keep it sealed and away from light.
description:
Oregano tea is a plain infusion of the dried herb, known as rigani in Greek and dushitsa in Russian. The same plant serves as a spice and a medicinal herb.

There is no real craft in the making: the plant is dried and crumbled. The flavour comes from its essential oil, which is sharp, with thymol and carvacrol among its main components. That oil is why a small amount goes a long way.

Expect something savoury and warming rather than sweet. Five minutes in just-boiled water is a good start, and longer pushes it towards bitter. Ground oregano is the common mistake: it is too fine and makes a gritty, harsh cup.

When buying, look for whole sprigs or coarse leaf with a strong smell when rubbed between your fingers. Avoid it during pregnancy, as is commonly advised. For something related but rarer, try Dittany of Crete, a cousin from the same genus.
history: Little is documented about oregano tea as a distinct drink. The plant itself is recorded as a medicinal herb and a spice, and in Russia also as a good honey plant.
sources_note: Harvest and colour notes are typical of the herb class, not specific reports.
